title_en: The Difference Between islām and īmān
body_ar:
لقد فسر رسول الله (ص) الإيمان في حديث وفد عبد القيس بما فسر به الإسلام في حديث جبريل فما وجه الجمع بين التفسيرين؟

أن الإيمان والإسلام لفظان شرعيان إذا اجتمعا افترقا وإذا افترقا اجتمعا، فإذا جاءا في سياق واحد اختلف معناهما كحديث جبريل، وإذا جاءا في سياقين مختلفين اتحد معناهما كحديث وفد عبد القيس،

فإن حديث وفد عبد القيس حين قالوا لرسول الله (ص) إنا لا نصل إليك إلا في الشهر الحرام وبيننا وبينك هذا الحي من كفار مضر فأمرنا بأمر فصل نعمل به ونخبر به من وراءنا وندخل به الجنة، فأمرهم بأربع ونهاهم عن أربع قال: «آمركم بالإيمان بالله وحده أتدرون ما الإيمان بالله وحده؟» وشرح لهم الإيمان بالله وحده بأن يشهدوا أن لا إله إلا الله وأن محمدا رسول الله ويقيموا الصلاة ويؤدوا خمس المغنم، وبين لهم الأربع التي يتركونها من الأشربة، فشرح لهم مفهوم الإيمان ببعض مفهوم الإسلام مما يدل على أن الإيمان والإسلام إذا جاءا منفردين اتحد معناهما،

أما إذا جاءا في سياق واحد كآية سورة الحجرات وهي قول الله تعالى: {قَالَتِ الْأَعْرَابُ آَمَنَّا قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا} [14] فإن معناهما يختلف كحديث جبريل، وكذلك حديث سعد بن أبي وقاص في الصحيحين أن رسول الله (ص) أعطى رجالا فترك رجلا وهو أعجبهم إلي فغلبني ما أعرف فيه، فقلت: يا رسول الله، مالك عن فلان فإني والله لأراه مؤمنا؟ فقال: أو مسلما، ففرق الرسول (ص) بين الكلمتين عندما وردتا في سياق واحد.
body_en:
The Messenger of God, upon whom be peace, explained faith (īmān) in the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays with the very thing by which he explained submission (islām) in the hadith of Gabriel. How are the two explanations to be reconciled?

Faith (īmān) and submission (islām) are two terms of the revealed law: when they are brought together they part, and when they are parted they come together. If they occur within a single context, their meanings differ, as in the hadith of Gabriel; and if they occur in two different contexts, their meaning is one, as in the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays.

As for the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays: when they said to the Messenger of God, upon whom be peace, 'We cannot reach you except in the sacred month, and between us and you is this clan of the unbelievers of Mudar, so command us with a decisive command which we may act upon and may pass on to those we have left behind, and by which we may enter the Garden' — he commanded them four things and forbade them four. He said: 'I command you to believe in God alone. Do you know what belief in God alone is?' And he explained belief in God alone to them as: that they bear witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, that they establish the prayer, and that they render a fifth of the spoils. And he set out for them the four things they were to abandon, among the drinks. So he explained the concept of īmān to them by part of the concept of islām — which shows that when īmān and islām occur singly, their meaning is one.

As for when they occur within a single context — like the verse of Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt, God's words, exalted is He: {The Bedouins said: we have believed. Say: you have not believed; rather say: we have submitted} (Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt 49:14) — then their meanings differ, as in the hadith of Gabriel. So too the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: that the Messenger of God, upon whom be peace, gave to a number of men and left out one man, who was the most pleasing of them to me; and what I knew of him overcame me, so I said: 'O Messenger of God, what is it with you and so-and-so? By God, I consider him a believer.' He said: 'Or a Muslim.' So the Messenger, upon whom be peace, distinguished between the two words when they occurred within a single context.

flags.context: وبين لهم الأربع التي يتركونها من الأشربة
options: the four things they were to abandon, among the drinks
the four drinking vessels they were to abandon
the four intoxicating drinks they were to abandon
flags.note: The Sheikh does not name the four, and the received wording of the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays lists four VESSELS (al-ḥantam, al-dubbāʾ, al-naqīr, al-muzaffat), not four drinks. His phrasing من الأشربة points to drinks. The English keeps his wording rather than substituting the familiar list, and the discrepancy is recorded here rather than resolved.

flags.arabic: إذا اجتمعا افترقا وإذا افترقا اجتمعا
flags.context: أن الإيمان والإسلام لفظان شرعيان إذا اجتمعا افترقا وإذا افترقا اجتمعا
options: when they are brought together they part, and when they are parted they come together
when they are mentioned together they differ, and when mentioned separately they coincide
united in expression they divide in meaning; divided in expression they unite in meaning
flags.note: A standing maxim of the usul tradition whose force lies in its symmetry. Option 0 keeps the shape at the cost of some immediate clarity; option 1 reads more plainly but loses the aphorism. The Sheikh's own gloss follows immediately in the text either way.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The source marks the Qur'anic quotation with its own brace brackets and gives only the bare verse number '[14]'; the sura name and full reference have been supplied in the English per house style, and the Arabic has not been altered.
The source writes the honorific as (ص) throughout. It is rendered in full in the English as 'upon whom be peace'.

In the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas the Sheikh moves mid-sentence from third-person narration into Saʿd's own first-person voice, exactly as the report runs. The shift has been kept rather than smoothed out.
The Sheikh attributes the hadith of Saʿd to 'the two Ṣaḥīḥs' and gives no grading for the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays or the hadith of Gabriel. No grading has been supplied.
